## Sixteen columns, one question per column

A busy groove gets legible the moment you give each instrument its own row on a
shared time grid. Sixteen steps cover one bar of 4/4 at four subdivisions per
beat. `true` means this instrument attacks in this column, `false` means
silence, and the array index becomes a time coordinate that every layer agrees
about.

Kick, snare and closed hi-hat are enough to start. Every extra sample you add
costs you another pattern decision, another balance decision and another timbral
decision before the pulse itself is settled. Separate rows also hand you a
reliable transcription method: loop one bar, listen for the snare and nothing
else, then go round again for the kick, then for the hat. You never have to hold
the whole kit in your attention at once.

Booleans record attacks and nothing more. Accents live in a parallel amplitude
array; feel lives in a small sleep offset that pushes one layer just behind the
strict subdivision. Keeping both in code is what makes a groove inspectable. An
audio loop preserves the feel perfectly and tells you nothing about which part
of that feel came from position, from accent, or from microtiming.

## Kick, snare and hat on one grid

The hat marks all sixteen subdivisions. Kick and snare take fewer, structurally
stronger columns. A four-value amplitude pattern gives each group of hats a
clear first step, and the hat thread delays its attacks by 0.02 beats while kick
and snare stay exactly on the grid. That offset is tiny. Do you expect to hear
it as a change in the pocket, or not at all?

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 100

kick =  [true, false, false, false, false, false, true, false,
         true, false, false, false, false, false, false, false]
snare = [false, false, false, false, true, false, false, false,
         false, false, false, false, true, false, false, false]
hats =  [true, true, true, true, true, true, true, true,
         true, true, true, true, true, true, true, true]
hat_amp = [0.8, 0.35, 0.5, 0.35] * 4

16.times do |step|
  sample :bd_haus, amp: 1.0 if kick[step]
  sample :sn_dub, amp: 0.8 if snare[step]

  in_thread do
    sleep 0.02
    sample :drum_cymbal_closed, amp: hat_amp[step], release: 0.08 if hats[step]
  end

  sleep 0.25
end
```

One bar takes 2.4 seconds, so wrap it in a `4.times do` loop while you listen.
The kick states beats 1 and 3 and adds a pickup on the subdivision just before
beat 3. Snare hits beats 2 and 4. Over the top of both, the hat lays down a
continuous sixteenth-note surface whose accents keep telling you where the four
big beats are.

## Flatten the accents, then move a hit

1. Set every hat amplitude to 0.5. Sixteenths keep coming at the same speed, and
   their grouping into four beats goes vague. Put the accent array back before
   you move a hit, so accent and position never change in the same comparison.
2. Move the second kick from index 6 to index 7. That attack now falls one
   sixteenth before beat 3, leaving a smaller gap to the downbeat kick. Listen
   for the forward pull the shorter gap creates.
3. Raise the hat delay from 0.02 to 0.06 beats. The hats peel away from kick and
   snare, and somewhere on the way they stop sounding relaxed and start sounding
   late. Back the number down until you hear the pocket shift without losing the
   sense of one coordinated kit.

## Why the accent row is separate data

Each row behaves like a Boolean function over the step number. At every column,
the renderer asks kick, snare and hat the same question: are you attacking now?
A shared index aligns the layers while letting their patterns differ completely.
It also gives you a paper method. Draw sixteen columns, mark one instrumental
row per listening pass, and copy the marks straight into arrays.

Amplitude has to be its own row because identical attack positions can carry
completely different metrical meanings. Equal hats preserve the subdivision and
flatten the beat structure above it. Stronger quarter-note positions orient your
ear; weaker subdivisions carry motion between them. Explicit numbers let a later
reader see that hierarchy without having to infer it from a mixed recording.

Microtiming comes last, once the strict grid is dependable. Delaying the hat
changes its relation to kick and snare anchors that haven't moved. Give all
three rows independent offsets before their columns are settled and a misplaced
attack sounds exactly like a stylistic delay. Keep a strict version so every
feel edit has a reference.

Isolation is what makes repeated listening productive. Mark the snare, then the
kick, then the hats, muting whatever you aren't reviewing. When you put the rows
back together, listen for composite accents: three instruments landing on one
column produce a weight that wasn't audible in any single layer.

## Transcribe a bar you can check

Take one bar of a groove you may legally inspect, or record a groove of your
own. Build one sixteen-step row per instrument, plus a parallel amplitude row
wherever the accents vary. Work in separate listening passes, and put a `REVIEW`
comment above any column you're unsure of, with the source time that raised the
doubt.

Get the readable grid reproducing the attacks first. Then add timing offsets in
a separate rendering path and keep the strict version alive beside it. That's
how you'll be able to say which of your changes belong to feel and which belong
to transcription.
